title: Partition of India in World Context

cards.h: A line drawn in a few weeks
cards.b:
In August 1947 the British Raj ended, and British India was divided into two new states, India and Pakistan. Pakistan was made up of two wings, east and west, separated by over a thousand miles of Indian land.

Partition was one of the largest and most violent migrations in modern history. It shaped the politics of South Asia for the rest of the century, and it remains a source of pain for millions of families.

cards.h: Two nations and a British exit
cards.b:
The Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah demanded a separate homeland for Muslims. The Indian National Congress, led by Nehru and Patel, wanted a united India. Britain, under growing pressure after the Second World War, decided to leave by 1947.

The Indian Independence Act was passed in July 1947. It set the date for independence at 15 August. Power was transferred to two dominions, and the princely states were left to choose their path.

The border between India and Pakistan was drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, a British barrister who had never been to India before. He had only a few weeks to draw the line through Bengal and Punjab. The final award was announced on 17 August 1947, two days after independence.

Many people had no idea which country they would live in until the lines were published. Radcliffe's decision divided villages, canal systems and cities.

cards.h: Urvashi Butalia and the other side of silence
cards.b:
Urvashi Butalia, The Other Side of Silence (1998)

Butalia collected stories from families who lived through partition. She shows how women, children and village communities were affected, and how many people never spoke about the violence.

Oral histories like this add a human layer to the political story.
The formal end of British rule was quick, but the social upheaval lasted for years. Millions moved across new borders in just a few months.

Hindus and Sikhs moved from the west Punjab towards India. Muslims moved from India towards Pakistan. Trains, convoys and foot columns carried people in huge numbers, and many were attacked on the way.

Estimates of the number of people who moved run to roughly ten to fifteen million. Estimates of those killed vary widely, from around two hundred thousand to over a million. Historians argue about the exact numbers.

Many textbooks treat partition as a natural result of religious difference that could not be avoided. The story suggests that two nations had always been separate.

Historians argue that partition was the result of choices made by political leaders, the British and local crowds. Communal violence in the 1940s, the design of the British exit and the struggle for power all played a part. The idea of inevitability hides those choices.

About 565 princely states had nominal independence within British India. Their rulers had to choose whether to join India or Pakistan. Hyderabad, Junagadh and Kashmir were the most contested. Hyderabad was taken over by Indian forces in 1948.

Kashmir led to war between India and Pakistan in 1947 and 1948. The dispute is still unresolved and remains one of the most sensitive issues in South Asia.

The partition of India was part of a wave of partitions after the Second World War. Ireland had been divided in 1921, and the UN recommended the partition of Palestine in November 1947. The pattern of drawing borders to meet political goals shaped much of the twentieth century.

Historians compare the cases to see what they share. Partition often produced mass movements of people, and it often left a lasting legacy of conflict and memory.

Mahatma Gandhi opposed partition and worked for communal peace in Bengal and Delhi. In January 1948 he began a fast in Delhi to stop the violence. Later that month he was assassinated by a Hindu extremist, Nathuram Godse.

Gandhi's death shocked India and the world. Historians argue about his role in the partition process, and his legacy in peace-making remains a strong part of public memory.

Partition left two states with strong national identities and deep mistrust. Wars were fought in 1947, 1965, 1971 and 1999, and the Kashmir issue has never been settled. At the same time, shared language, food and music continue across the border.

The memory of partition is kept alive in novels, films and family stories. It is one of the central events of the modern history of South Asia.

India became a republic in 1950, when its new Constitution came into force. The Constituent Assembly had begun its work in 1946 and included many voices from across the country, though it was dominated by Congress.

The new state had to settle refugees, rebuild cities, and bring the princely states into the union. The Constitution's promise of equality was tested by the scale of the displacement and the violence.

Five things to remember
  1. India and Pakistan became independent on 14 and 15 August 1947.
  2. Cyril Radcliffe drew the boundary line.
  3. Millions moved across the new border.
  4. Estimates of the dead vary widely.
  5. Kashmir remains disputed.
Think about it
  • Was partition a choice or a result of deeper forces?
  • How should a nation remember a violent birth?
